title: Arbitration: seat, arbitrability, appointment and review
summary: The modern Indian move toward seat-centred arbitration, limited court intervention and structurally impartial tribunals.

steps.title: BALCO v Kaiser Aluminium Technical Services Inc
steps.holding: The Constitution Bench adopted the territoriality principle and held prospectively that Part I does not apply to foreign-seated arbitrations, subject to later statutory amendments for limited interim support.

steps.title: Booz Allen and Hamilton Inc v SBI Home Finance Ltd
steps.holding: The Court distinguished rights in personam from rights in rem and held that mortgage enforcement through sale was not arbitrable in the circumstances.

steps.title: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC v HSCC (India) Ltd
steps.holding: The Court held that a person interested in the outcome cannot retain exclusive power to appoint the sole arbitrator.

steps.title: Vidya Drolia v Durga Trading Corporation
steps.holding: The Court formulated a fourfold non-arbitrability test and adopted a restrained prima facie referral review, while treating certain rent disputes under special statutes differently from ordinary tenancy claims.

steps.title: Ssangyong Engineering & Construction Co Ltd v National Highways Authority of India
steps.holding: The Court narrowed public-policy review, explained patent illegality for domestic awards and set aside the relevant part because the tribunal effectively created a new bargain contrary to the contract and natural justice.

steps.title: N N Global Mercantile Pvt Ltd v Indo Unique Flame Ltd
steps.holding: The majority held that non-stamping is a curable defect and does not render the arbitration agreement void or non-existent; referral courts should not derail arbitration through a full stamp inquiry.

steps.title: PASL Wind Solutions Pvt Ltd v GE Power Conversion India Pvt Ltd
steps.holding: Party autonomy permits Indian parties to choose a foreign seat absent a specific statutory prohibition; an award made there can be a foreign award, while mandatory Indian law may still affect the underlying transaction and available relief.

title: Arrest, bail and personal liberty
summary: The gradual construction of safeguards against routine arrest, custodial abuse and prolonged pre-trial detention.

steps.title: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v State of Punjab
steps.holding: The Court rejected inflexible formulas, treated anticipatory bail as protection of liberty through judicial discretion and required attention to the facts, seriousness, flight risk and misuse.

steps.title: D K Basu v State of West Bengal
steps.holding: The Court prescribed arrest, documentation, notification, medical examination and production safeguards, treating non-compliance as actionable and potentially contemptuous.

steps.title: Arnesh Kumar v State of Bihar
steps.holding: The Court directed police to justify arrest through statutory factors and magistrates to scrutinise detention rather than approve it mechanically.

steps.title: Sushila Aggarwal v State (NCT of Delhi)
steps.holding: Anticipatory bail need not ordinarily be time-bound and can continue until the end of trial, though courts may impose justified conditions or duration in a particular case.

steps.title: Satender Kumar Antil v Central Bureau of Investigation
steps.holding: The Court issued category-based directions, emphasised compliance with arrest safeguards, timely bail disposal and legislative consideration of a comprehensive bail law.

steps.title: Pankaj Bansal v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court required written communication of the grounds so that the arrested person can meaningfully challenge detention and seek bail.

title: Basic structure and limited constitutional amendment
summary: How an initially broad amendment power became subject to judicially enforceable limits protecting constitutional identity.

steps.title: His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v State of Kerala
steps.holding: Parliament's amending power is wide but cannot damage or destroy the Constitution's basic structure. The opinions differed on detail, but the basic-structure limitation became the controlling proposition.

steps.title: Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain
steps.holding: The Court invalidated the immunity provision through basic-structure reasoning, emphasising free and fair elections, equality and judicial review.

steps.title: Minerva Mills Ltd v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court held that limited amending power and the harmony between fundamental rights and Directive Principles are features of the basic structure.

steps.title: I R Coelho v State of Tamil Nadu
steps.holding: The Court held that post-24 April 1973 Ninth Schedule laws remain reviewable where their impact damages basic-structure principles reflected in fundamental rights.

steps.title: Janhit Abhiyan v Union of India
steps.holding: A majority upheld the amendment; the dissent disagreed particularly with exclusion. The decision accepts economic criteria for the new constitutional category.

title: Civil procedure: jurisdiction, finality and case management
summary: The procedural system from valid forum and finality to default, amendment, ADR and threshold rejection.

steps.title: Kiran Singh v Chaman Paswan
steps.holding: A defect of subject-matter or inherent jurisdiction strikes at the court's authority and ordinarily renders the decree a nullity. Statutory rules may restrict late objections to territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction by requiring timely objection and consequent failure of justice.

steps.title: Satyadhyan Ghosal v Deorajin Debi
steps.holding: The principle of finality can apply between stages of the same litigation so that an issue finally decided at an earlier stage is not ordinarily reopened at a later stage, subject to appellate correction and the procedural setting.

steps.title: Sangram Singh v Election Tribunal, Kotah
steps.holding: Procedure is designed to advance justice rather than create traps, but a court must still respect the text, the stage reached, the other side's accrued procedural position and the conditions for setting aside default.

steps.title: Salem Advocate Bar Association, Tamil Nadu v Union of India (II)
steps.holding: The Court upheld and operationalised major procedural reforms, issued implementation guidance and treated case management, realistic costs and ADR referral as tools for reducing delay while preserving fairness.

steps.title: Revajeetu Builders and Developers v Narayanaswamy and Sons
steps.holding: Courts should consider whether the amendment is necessary for the real controversy, bona fide, compensable in costs, prejudicial beyond repair, limitation-sensitive or transformative of the case; the post-trial due-diligence requirement must also be respected.

steps.title: Dahiben v Arvindbhai Kalyanji Bhanusali
steps.holding: The court examines the plaint as a whole and the documents relied on by the plaintiff, assuming pleaded facts for the limited inquiry; a clever drafting device cannot avoid rejection where the bar is apparent, but disputed defence material is not tried at this stage.

title: Competition enforcement and sector regulation
summary: Institutional jurisdiction, cartel penalties and coordination between competition and sector regulators.

steps.title: Competition Commission of India v Steel Authority of India Ltd
steps.holding: The Court treated the prima facie investigation direction as administrative and non-appealable at that stage, while explaining CCI procedure and later hearing rights.

steps.title: Excel Crop Care Ltd v Competition Commission of India
steps.holding: The Court sustained the cartel findings and held that penalty should ordinarily be calculated on relevant turnover rather than total enterprise turnover.

steps.title: Competition Commission of India v Bharti Airtel Ltd
steps.holding: The Court required foundational technical issues within TRAI's domain to be determined first, after which the CCI could examine competition-law consequences.

title: Contract interpretation, frustration and damages
summary: How Indian contract law distinguishes construction, implied terms, supervening impossibility and compensation.

steps.title: Satyabrata Ghose v Mugneeram Bangur & Co
steps.holding: Impossibility includes impracticability that strikes at the foundation of the bargain, but the requisition on the facts did not necessarily frustrate the contract.

steps.title: Fateh Chand v Balkishan Das
steps.holding: Section 74 awards reasonable compensation up to the named amount; it does not permit automatic recovery or forfeiture disconnected from breach and legally cognisable loss.

steps.title: Kailash Nath Associates v Delhi Development Authority
steps.holding: The Court held that forfeiture requires breach and reasonable compensation; where loss is capable of proof it should be proved, and a public authority cannot retain money arbitrarily.

steps.title: Energy Watchdog v Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
steps.holding: The Court held that a mere rise in cost does not frustrate a contract; the force-majeure clause and contractual allocation of risk govern before section 56 is considered.

steps.title: Nabha Power Ltd v Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd
steps.holding: A term may be implied only where strict necessity and the recognised business-efficacy conditions are met; courts should not rewrite a negotiated commercial instrument.

title: Copyright: expression, originality and user rights
summary: The development of idea-expression separation, originality, educational use and moral rights.

steps.title: R G Anand v Deluxe Films
steps.holding: Copyright does not protect a general idea, theme or subject; infringement depends on substantial similarity in protected expression assessed through the overall impression and material similarities.

steps.title: Eastern Book Company v D B Modak
steps.holding: The Court rejected pure sweat of the brow and required creativity in the selection or arrangement, while recognising protection for qualifying editorial contributions but not the underlying judgments.

steps.title: The Chancellor, Masters & Scholars of the University of Oxford v Rameshwari Photocopy Services
steps.holding: The Division Bench adopted a broad reading of use in the course of instruction and rejected infringement on the facts, while emphasising the educational setting.

steps.title: Amar Nath Sehgal v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court recognised strong moral-right protection against distortion, mutilation and destruction prejudicial to the artist's honour and reputation.

title: Corporate personality, veil piercing, governance and insolvency
summary: The path from separate legal personality to controlled veil piercing, minority protection and insolvency resolution.

steps.title: Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd
steps.holding: The company was a separate legal person with its own rights and liabilities, notwithstanding concentrated ownership.

steps.title: Life Insurance Corporation of India v Escorts Ltd
steps.holding: The Court recognised that veil lifting is exceptional and depends on statute, fraud, evasion, agency or the demands of the particular legal rule; it is not a general licence to ignore incorporation.

steps.title: Delhi Development Authority v Skipper Construction Co
steps.holding: The Court disregarded the corporate structure to prevent fraud and enforce restitutionary and protective orders.

steps.title: Swiss Ribbons Pvt Ltd v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court substantially upheld the Code, treating insolvency resolution rather than debt recovery as its central objective and accepting differentiated treatment based on relevant economic roles.

steps.title: Tata Consultancy Services Ltd v Cyrus Investments Pvt Ltd
steps.holding: The Court restored the NCLT's dismissal, emphasising the statutory threshold for oppression and the limits of substituting judicial business judgment for lawful corporate governance.

title: Daughters, coparcenary and women's property
summary: The shift from restricted female property interests toward equal coparcenary rights and absolute ownership.

steps.title: V Tulasamma v Sesha Reddy
steps.holding: Property possessed in recognition of a pre-existing right is enlarged under section 14(1); section 14(2) is confined to a genuinely new restricted grant.

steps.title: Prakash v Phulavati
steps.holding: The decision adopted a prospective approach requiring the father to be alive. That proposition was later displaced by Vineeta Sharma.

steps.title: Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma
steps.holding: The Court held that the right is by birth and does not depend on the father's survival on the commencement date, while protecting certain completed partitions.

title: Delhi rent control: tenancy, need and appellate occupation
summary: Heritability, summary leave, bona fide need, constitutional extension and occupation charges during appeal.

steps.title: Gian Devi Anand v Jeevan Kumar
steps.holding: In the absence of a contrary statutory provision, tenancy rights and statutory protection are generally heritable; residential and commercial tenancies cannot be differentiated merely by judicial assumption.

steps.title: Precision Steel and Engineering Works v Prem Deva Niranjan Deva Tayal
steps.holding: The tenant need not prove the defence at the leave stage; an affidavit disclosing facts which, if proved, would disentitle the landlord or raise a genuine triable issue requires a trial.

steps.title: Shiv Sarup Gupta v Dr Mahesh Chand Gupta
steps.holding: The court examines the landlord's genuine, honest need from a practical perspective while testing objective facts, the nature of the premises and reasonably suitable alternative accommodation; the tenant cannot dictate the landlord's lifestyle, but the claim is not immune from scrutiny.

steps.title: Satyawati Sharma v Union of India
steps.holding: The discriminatory exclusion of commercial premises from the landlord-need remedy was read down so that the provision operated without the irrational distinction.

steps.title: Atma Ram Properties (P) Ltd v Federal Motors (P) Ltd
steps.holding: A stay can be conditioned on reasonable compensation for continued occupation after the eviction decree, reflecting the landlord's lost use rather than freezing payment at historic contractual rent.

title: Digital speech, privacy and open justice
summary: A trail from publication privacy to intermediary speech restrictions, constitutional privacy and internet shutdown review.

steps.title: R Rajagopal v State of Tamil Nadu
steps.holding: The Court recognised a privacy interest against unauthorised publication of private life but protected publication based on public records and rejected prior restraint by officials.

steps.title: Shreya Singhal v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court struck down section 66A for vagueness and overbreadth, upheld section 69A with safeguards and read actual knowledge for intermediary takedown as requiring court or authorised governmental process.

steps.title: Justice K S Puttaswamy (Retd) v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court unanimously recognised privacy as an intrinsic part of life, liberty and the freedoms in Part III, while explaining that restrictions require legality, legitimate aim and proportional safeguards.

steps.title: Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court held that freedom of speech and trade through the internet receive constitutional protection, indefinite suspension is impermissible, orders must be published and restrictions require periodic proportionality review.

title: Elections, democracy and political transparency
summary: From electoral adjudication and Election Commission authority to candidate disclosure, disqualification, political finance and voter-roll review.

steps.title: Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain
steps.holding: The Court invalidated the immunity provision through basic-structure reasoning, emphasising free and fair elections, equality and judicial review.

steps.title: Mohinder Singh Gill v Chief Election Commissioner
steps.holding: The Court recognised broad residual election-management power within law and stated that an order must stand or fall on the reasons contained in it, not later affidavits.

steps.title: Union of India v Association for Democratic Reforms
steps.holding: The Court held that informed voting is protected by Article 19(1)(a) and directed disclosure of specified candidate information.

steps.title: Lily Thomas v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court invalidated the protection, making disqualification operate from conviction subject to lawful appellate relief.

steps.title: Keisham Meghachandra Singh v Hon'ble Speaker, Manipur Legislative Assembly
steps.holding: The Court directed time-bound adjudication and suggested reconsideration of the Speaker's institutional role, reflecting concern about strategic delay.

steps.title: Association for Democratic Reforms v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court invalidated the scheme and connected amendments, holding that the information restrictions were disproportionate and that unlimited corporate contributions created serious equality concerns.

steps.title: Association for Democratic Reforms v Election Commission of India
steps.holding: The Court upheld the revision, treated Article 324 and the Representation of the People Act as complementary, recognised a limited electoral-eligibility inquiry into citizenship and required referral of final citizenship determination to the competent authority.

title: Electronic evidence, authentication and source integrity
summary: How Indian evidence law moved toward mandatory electronic-record certification while confronting authenticity and fabricated authority.

steps.title: Anvar P V v P K Basheer
steps.holding: The Court required compliance with the electronic-record certificate provision for the relevant category of secondary electronic evidence and displaced contrary reasoning in State v Navjot Sandhu.

steps.title: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
steps.holding: The Court reaffirmed the certificate requirement for secondary electronic evidence, clarified that it may be produced at an appropriate stage and recognised court assistance where the record is controlled by another person.

steps.title: Pooja Ramesh Singh v Jammu and Kashmir Bank Ltd
steps.holding: The Court set aside the tainted decisions, held that a decision infected by fabricated precedent cannot stand, adopted zero tolerance for unverified hallucinated authority and directed the Bar Council of India to consider professional standards.

title: Environmental liability, precaution and restorative remedies
summary: The movement from common-law strict liability to absolute enterprise liability, sustainable development and expert review.

steps.title: Rylands v Fletcher
steps.holding: The defendant may be liable for non-natural use, accumulation and escape, subject to recognised exceptions.

steps.title: M C Mehta v Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak)
steps.holding: The Court formulated absolute and non-delegable enterprise liability, without the traditional Rylands exceptions, and linked compensation to the enterprise's capacity and the magnitude of harm.

steps.title: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court treated sustainable development, precaution and polluter pays as part of Indian environmental law and ordered remedial and compensation measures.

steps.title: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court imposed responsibility for remediation on the offending industries and reinforced polluter-pays and absolute-liability reasoning.

steps.title: A P Pollution Control Board v M V Nayudu
steps.holding: The Court emphasised precaution, the limits of conventional adjudication and the need for expert environmental decision-making.

steps.title: Hanuman Laxman Aroskar v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court required reasoned, transparent and informed appraisal, treated environmental rule of law as central and suspended the clearance for reconsideration.

title: Substantive equality and reservation doctrine
summary: The development of backward-class identification, creamy layer, promotion, economic criteria and sub-classification.

steps.title: Indra Sawhney v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court upheld OBC reservation, required exclusion of the creamy layer, generally limited reservation to fifty per cent and rejected reservation in promotion under the then text.

steps.title: Jarnail Singh v Lachhmi Narain Gupta
steps.holding: The Court removed the requirement to collect data proving backwardness of SCs and STs, while retaining other constitutional requirements and applying the creamy-layer principle to exclude the advanced.

steps.title: Janhit Abhiyan v Union of India
steps.holding: A majority upheld the amendment; the dissent disagreed particularly with exclusion. The decision accepts economic criteria for the new constitutional category.

steps.title: State of Punjab v Davinder Singh
steps.holding: The Court held that sub-classification is permissible when supported by relevant data and directed toward more effective distribution of benefits; individual opinions differed on aspects such as creamy layer.

title: Foreign judgments, forum choice and arbitral awards
summary: Indian conflict-of-laws doctrine on foreign divorce, anti-suit relief, judgment recognition and award enforcement.

steps.title: Satya v Teja Singh
steps.holding: A foreign judgment founded on a fraudulent assumption of jurisdiction or denial of a real opportunity to contest is not entitled to recognition merely because it is formally valid in the foreign forum.

steps.title: Y Narasimha Rao v Y Venkata Lakshmi
steps.holding: Recognition ordinarily requires jurisdiction and a ground of relief recognised by the matrimonial law governing the parties, a decision on merits, fair notice and opportunity, and absence of fraud or breach of Indian law.

steps.title: Modi Entertainment Network v WSG Cricket Pte Ltd
steps.holding: An anti-suit injunction is an equitable order against a party, not the foreign court. It requires personal jurisdiction, caution, comity, prevention of injustice and a strong case that the chosen foreign proceeding is oppressive, vexatious or contrary to a binding forum arrangement.

steps.title: Renusagar Power Co Ltd v General Electric Co
steps.holding: For foreign awards, public policy was confined to fundamental policy, the interests of India and justice or morality, rather than a merits review. Later legislation and cases refined the language but preserved a narrow enforcement orientation.

steps.title: Alcon Electronics Pvt Ltd v Celem SA
steps.holding: A judgment from a competent foreign court may be conclusive and executable when it is on merits and does not fall within the statutory exceptions concerning natural justice, fraud, incorrect jurisdictional foundation or breach of Indian law.

steps.title: PASL Wind Solutions Pvt Ltd v GE Power Conversion India Pvt Ltd
steps.holding: Party autonomy permits Indian parties to choose a foreign seat absent a specific statutory prohibition; an award made there can be a foreign award, while mandatory Indian law may still affect the underlying transaction and available relief.

title: Gender, sexuality and decisional autonomy
summary: A trail connecting workplace equality, gender identity, sexual orientation, marriage, bodily autonomy and reproductive choice.

steps.title: Vishaka v State of Rajasthan
steps.holding: The Court held that workplace sexual harassment violates equality, dignity, liberty and occupational freedom, used international norms consistent with fundamental rights, and issued binding guidelines until legislation was enacted.

steps.title: National Legal Services Authority v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court recognised transgender persons as entitled to constitutional equality, dignity and self-identification, and directed affirmative governmental measures.

steps.title: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court invalidated section 377 to the extent it criminalised consensual adult intimacy, while leaving non-consensual acts and acts involving minors outside that protection.

steps.title: Joseph Shine v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court struck down the offence as arbitrary, discriminatory and incompatible with dignity and sexual autonomy, while clarifying that adultery may remain relevant in civil matrimonial law.

steps.title: Independent Thought v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court read down the exception so that intercourse with a wife below eighteen falls within the rape offence, harmonising criminal, child-protection and marriage laws.

steps.title: X v Principal Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department, Government of NCT of Delhi
steps.holding: The Court interpreted the law inclusively, rejected marital-status discrimination and connected reproductive choice with dignity, privacy and changing family forms.

title: International criminal law and refugee protection
summary: Classification of conflict, individual criminal responsibility and the protection of people fleeing persecution.

steps.title: Prosecutor v Dusko Tadic (Jurisdiction Decision)
steps.court: International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia
steps.holding: The Appeals Chamber articulated a broad armed-conflict threshold and upheld the tribunal's establishment and jurisdiction.

steps.title: Prosecutor v Jean-Paul Akayesu
steps.holding: The Trial Chamber entered the first international conviction for genocide and recognised rape and sexual violence as capable of constituting acts of genocide when committed with the required intent.

steps.title: Prosecutor v Thomas Lubanga Dyilo
steps.holding: The ICC convicted Lubanga and later developed victim-participation and reparation principles, while debate continued about charging strategy and sexual violence evidence.

steps.title: National Human Rights Commission v State of Arunachal Pradesh
steps.holding: The Court required protection of life and liberty, restrained forcible eviction except through lawful process and directed authorities to process citizenship applications according to law.

steps.title: Louis De Raedt v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court recognised Article 21 protection but held that the citizen-specific right to reside and settle does not extend to foreigners, whose stay remains governed by law.

title: International organisations: personality, powers and immunity
summary: The development of institutional personality, implied powers, budgetary authority, staff justice and functional immunity.

steps.title: Reparation for Injuries Suffered in the Service of the United Nations
steps.holding: The Court recognised objective international personality and powers necessary for the organisation to perform its functions.

steps.title: Effect of Awards of Compensation Made by the United Nations Administrative Tribunal
steps.holding: The organisation's constituent framework and implied powers supported creation of an independent tribunal whose final awards bound the organisation; institutional effectiveness and justice for staff required legal effect.

steps.title: Certain Expenses of the United Nations
steps.holding: The Court treated peacekeeping expenditures undertaken to fulfil UN purposes as organisational expenses, while distinguishing Security Council and General Assembly competences.

steps.title: Difference Relating to Immunity from Legal Process of a Special Rapporteur of the Commission on Human Rights
steps.holding: Functional immunity attaches to words and acts performed in the course of the mission, and the competent United Nations determination carries substantial weight; the host state must respect treaty obligations and available settlement procedures.

steps.title: Legal Consequences for States of the Continued Presence of South Africa in Namibia
steps.holding: South Africa's continued presence was illegal; states were obliged not to recognise or assist the unlawful situation while taking account of the interests of Namibia's people.

title: Legal personality beyond the individual human
summary: How Indian law uses juristic personality for deities, considers animal interests and experiments with nature personhood.

steps.title: Yogendra Nath Naskar v Commissioner of Income Tax
steps.holding: A consecrated deity may be recognised as a juristic person capable of holding property and being represented through a human manager, with legal personality serving the purposes of the endowment.

steps.title: Ram Jankijee Deities v State of Bihar
steps.holding: The juristic deity acts through a human representative, and courts distinguish the legal person, the physical idol and the manager who protects the endowed property.

steps.title: Animal Welfare Board of India v A Nagaraja
steps.holding: Animal-welfare statutes must be applied to prevent unnecessary pain and protect animal well-being; constitutional duties and an ecocentric approach may inform interpretation, although the precise constitutional status of animal rights remains doctrinally contested and later legislation must be checked.

steps.title: Mohd Salim v State of Uttarakhand
steps.holding: The High Court used juristic personality as a protective device, but the order's operation and practical implications were questioned and stayed in later Supreme Court proceedings. It should be studied as an ambitious but unsettled personhood experiment.

steps.title: M Siddiq (D) through LRs v Mahant Suresh Das
steps.holding: The Court treated the deity as a juristic person, assessed documentary and archaeological evidence, distinguished faith from proof of title, and fashioned relief through the law of property and constitutional authority.

title: From formal procedure to liberty, dignity and privacy
summary: The constitutional transformation from isolated rights and formal legality to integrated, fair and proportionate rights review.

steps.title: A K Gopalan v State of Madras
steps.holding: The majority treated the rights as largely separate and read 'procedure established by law' narrowly. The compartmental approach was displaced by later decisions, especially R C Cooper and Maneka Gandhi.

steps.title: R C Cooper v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court focused on the direct effect of the measure and rejected rigid compartmentalisation of fundamental rights.

steps.title: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court held that procedure under Article 21 cannot be arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive; it must satisfy fairness and be tested with Articles 14 and 19 where engaged. Natural-justice requirements may be implied even when a statute is silent.

steps.title: Justice K S Puttaswamy (Retd) v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court unanimously recognised privacy as an intrinsic part of life, liberty and the freedoms in Part III, while explaining that restrictions require legality, legitimate aim and proportional safeguards.

steps.title: Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court held that freedom of speech and trade through the internet receive constitutional protection, indefinite suspension is impermissible, orders must be published and restrictions require periodic proportionality review.

title: Muslim marriage, divorce and post-divorce maintenance
summary: The interaction of personal law, statutory interpretation, constitutional equality and maintenance remedies.

steps.title: Mohd Ahmed Khan v Shah Bano Begum
steps.holding: The Court held that the remedy applied irrespective of religion and that the husband's personal-law obligations did not exclude the statutory duty.

steps.title: Danial Latifi v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court upheld the Act by construing it to require a fair provision made within iddat that can meet the divorced woman's future needs beyond that period.

steps.title: Shamim Ara v State of Uttar Pradesh
steps.holding: A mere assertion in a written statement is insufficient; talaq must be proved as pronounced for reasonable cause and preceded by an attempt at reconciliation in the framework adopted by the Court.

steps.title: Shayara Bano v Union of India
steps.holding: A majority set aside talaq-e-biddat, though the judges used different routes, including arbitrariness and the status of the practice within personal law.

title: Patents, pharmaceuticals and public-interest limits
summary: How patentability, incremental innovation and infringement remedies interact with access and competition.

steps.title: Novartis AG v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court rejected the claim because the evidence did not establish enhanced therapeutic efficacy over the known substance and carefully distinguished patentability from general improvement.

steps.title: F Hoffmann-La Roche Ltd v Cipla Ltd
steps.holding: The appellate judgment applied purposive claim construction and analysed infringement separately from validity, while addressing obviousness and public-interest arguments.

title: Professional ethics, advocacy and source verification
summary: Duties to client and court, custody of files, strikes, courtroom misconduct and AI-assisted authority verification.

steps.title: V C Rangadurai v D Gopalan
steps.holding: The Court stressed that advocacy is a public profession founded on trust and tailored the sanction while requiring restitution and ethical accountability.

steps.title: R D Saxena v Balram Prasad Sharma
steps.holding: The Court held that an advocate has no lien over the client's case papers and must return them, subject to lawful fee remedies.

steps.title: Ex-Capt Harish Uppal v Union of India
steps.holding: The Court held that lawyers have no right to strike or give a call for boycott, subject only to an extremely narrow symbolic protest in the rarest circumstances.

steps.title: R K Anand v Registrar, Delhi High Court
steps.holding: The Court upheld contempt findings, examined professional misconduct and stressed the duty of advocates to preserve trial integrity.

steps.title: Pooja Ramesh Singh v Jammu and Kashmir Bank Ltd
steps.holding: The Court set aside the tainted decisions, held that a decision infected by fabricated precedent cannot stand, adopted zero tolerance for unverified hallucinated authority and directed the Bar Council of India to consider professional standards.

title: Statutory interpretation: text, context, purpose and restraint
summary: A trail across mischief, penal strictness, whole-statute reading, purposive tax interpretation and limits on judicial supplementation.

steps.title: Bengal Immunity Co Ltd v State of Bihar
steps.holding: The prior law, defect or mischief, legislative remedy and reason for the remedy may illuminate ambiguous text, while remaining anchored to the enacted words.

steps.title: Tolaram Relumal v State of Bombay
steps.holding: A penal provision should not be extended by implication; where two reasonable constructions remain after ordinary interpretation, the one avoiding penal liability is preferred.

steps.title: Reserve Bank of India v Peerless General Finance and Investment Co Ltd
steps.holding: Interpretation depends on the text and context together; a provision should be read as part of the entire statute, its scheme and purpose rather than as an isolated sentence.

steps.title: K P Varghese v Income Tax Officer
steps.holding: The Court used text, statutory purpose and legislative history to require proof of understatement rather than taxing a fictional receipt.

steps.title: Commissioner of Customs (Import), Mumbai v Dilip Kumar and Company
steps.holding: The claimant must establish that the exemption applies; unresolved ambiguity in an exemption notification is ordinarily construed in favour of the revenue, while ambiguity in the charging provision follows different principles.

steps.title: Rohitash Kumar v Om Prakash Sharma
steps.holding: Courts cannot ordinarily supply an omission or recast legislation merely because the result seems inconvenient; correction is exceptional and must be compelled by the statute read as a whole.

title: Tax avoidance, statutory substance and commercial structure
summary: The movement from anti-device rhetoric to disciplined application of enacted tax rules and genuine commercial arrangements.

steps.title: K P Varghese v Income Tax Officer
steps.holding: The Court used text, statutory purpose and legislative history to require proof of understatement rather than taxing a fictional receipt.

steps.title: McDowell and Co Ltd v Commercial Tax Officer
steps.holding: The judgments condemned colourable devices, but later authority clarified that legitimate tax planning remains permissible and that McDowell should not be read as a universal anti-avoidance rule.

steps.title: Union of India v Azadi Bachao Andolan
steps.holding: The Court upheld the circular and rejected the proposition that every tax-avoidance arrangement is illegitimate; legal form and treaty entitlement matter unless the law supplies a contrary rule.

steps.title: Vodafone International Holdings BV v Union of India
steps.holding: The majority held that the transaction fell outside the then statutory charge and emphasised legal structure absent sham; Parliament later enacted retrospective amendments.

title: Worker status, discipline and industrial remedies
summary: A trail from employment classification and industry definition to domestic inquiry, tribunal review and remedial restoration.

steps.title: Dharangadhra Chemical Works Ltd v State of Saurashtra
steps.holding: The Court treated control and supervision as important but assessed the real relationship rather than contractual labels.

steps.title: Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board v A Rajappa
steps.holding: The Court formulated the triple test of systematic activity, cooperation between employer and employee and production or distribution of goods or services for human wants, subject to limited sovereign-function exclusion.

steps.title: Workmen of Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co of India v Management
steps.holding: The Court explained when a tribunal may reappraise evidence, permit the employer to prove misconduct and examine punishment, principles later reflected in section 11A.

steps.title: Hindustan Tin Works Pvt Ltd v Employees
steps.holding: Reinstatement may ordinarily carry restoration of lost wages, but relief depends on the facts, including the nature of illegality, delay, gainful employment and equitable considerations; later law has made the inquiry more contextual.

steps.title: Jaipur Zila Sahakari Bhoomi Vikas Bank Ltd v Ram Gopal Sharma
steps.holding: Where statutory approval is required and refused or not obtained, the dismissal does not become legally effective in the manner contemplated by the provision, protecting the worker during pending proceedings.
